https://github.com/skbaek/blanc — https://skbaek.github.io/blanc/

Blanc is a minimal contract language for the EVM, written and proved in Lean 4. A program is raw EVM instructions under four constructors (branch/last/next/call); the compiler's one real job is placing jumps, and its correctness is itself a theorem — so every contract property is stated about the exact bytes that deploy. Underneath is Jaune, an executable EVM semantics in plain Lean 4 that passes all 5,100 supported files (34,005 cases) of the mainnet fixture corpus, Prague through BPO2, and answers as a standard t8n tool.

Four contracts so far — a WETH, an ERC-3156 flash-mint token, the full 27-selector WETH10, and a port of Lido's CircuitBreaker — with theorem kinds including:

  • solvency and supply-conservation invariants preserved over every reachable state of a configured chain: induction over whole blocks, across scheduled fork activations, and WETH's solvency carries no hash-collision hypothesis anywhere in its statement;
  • liveness by construction (WETH10): from a proved deployment root, at every reachable future, every admissible withdraw/withdrawTo succeeds — at message altitude and as a signed type-2 transaction;
  • flashLoan settlement with the borrower's code universally quantified — the interpreter is total, so no premise about the callee is needed;
  • exact gas as proved equations (e.g. totalSupply() = 2,218 gas).

CI pins each of 844 audited theorems to its exact axiom closure (nothing beyond propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; no native_decide), and differential gates run each contract beside EELS — 147/147 WETH10 rows, 175/175 CircuitBreaker rows. Most of the proofs were written by AI agents; the kernel doesn't care.

The bill is the language itself: new, deliberately bare, and austere to prove in — about 290,000 lines of Lean for those four contracts — and nothing here verifies contracts already deployed. Feedback would be highly appreciated, especially on what would be worth porting or proving next.

Hi, nice to see the announcement here, I've already read your library before, and I'm also experimenting with similar things with the help of coding agents, for example, https://github.com/yihuang/evm-abi-lean which is a evm abi encode/decode library that can prove the roundtrip property, and https://github.com/yihuang/evm-interpreter-verified an evm in evm interpreter verified in lean4 against a minimal EVM spec.
One thing I find in the process is that although the ai can do the proof, the size of the proof is magnitudes longer than the program itself, I wonder if that's some inherent complexity or we can do it better.
My intuitive understanding is that these program proofs are mostly mechanical, in the sense that there's no really hard math problem in it, most of the time we just need the right structure or abstraction and better tactic automations to keep it readable.
Keen to hear your experience and opinions on this.

Cool project, so this is essentially a verified EVM assembler?

Also curious: why did you choose to make & use Jaune instead of using the Nethermind or powdr/leonardoalt Lean4 EVM semantics?

@yi huang

Yes, "would the proofs be dramatically shorter/better if I wrote every line by hand?" is something I keep thinking about. I have been pushing agents hard to find and refactor bloat, but so far they seem to be more effective at making things faster than smaller.

There were some cases where alternative designs would have shortened specific parts by orders of magnitude. E.g., you can prove that an execution goes from state s1 to s2 by (1) defining execution as a relational predicate Exec and painstakingly building an enormous term of type Exec s1 s2, or (2) defining it as a definitionally reducing function exec and proving exec s1 = s2 by rfl (in practice it's a bit more messy, but you get the idea). But the latter approach has been mostly rejected so far because the loss of evaluation control was too steep a cost relative to gains in proof density.

So my tentative answer is: it's partly a deliberate trade rather than inherent complexity - the shorter proofs exist, but they don't come at attractive prices, at least not yet.

Also, since your gap-analysis already points at Jaune as the bridge target: if anything on the Jaune side would make that easier - the t8n interface for differential runs, or exposing whatever the projection needs - I'm happy to help with the integration. "Your workflow doesn't fit Jaune's API as-is" is exactly the kind of feedback I'm looking for at this stage.

@Philogy

Essentially yes - Blanc is an assembly-altitude language that imposes a very thin structure over raw EVM instructions, where the structure does double duty of (1) providing the rudiments of high-level programming (named functions, branching, recursion), and (2) taming the CFG for easier verification.

As for alternative specs, the historical reason is that they weren't around (or I couldn't find them) when I started - the closest thing I could find back then was Yoichi Hirai's Lem-based eth-isabelle, which was already unmaintained.

But even starting today, I think I'd lean toward something like Jaune, for two reasons.

First, there is a very specific feature set I want from a spec: complete executable conformance with current mainnet's supported fixtures, no trust base beyond 3 classical axioms (no native_decide, no FFI for precomps, etc.), bytecode-level semantics, exact gas for liveness theorems, etc. This isn't necessarily a better feature set, it's just what I want for my line of work (e.g. targeting Yul instead of EVM bytecode would be a perfectly good choice depending on your objectives), but the best way to ensure you'll always get what you want is building it yourself.

Second, owning the spec means owning its internals, and tiny representational choices there can pay surprising dividends for downstream proof work. E.g., a straightforward port of EELS gives you an 8-way mutual recursion for the execution core, which is fine if you're just running fixtures, but a royal pain the moment you try to relate it to an execution predicate. Because I control Jaune, I could sidestep that problem entirely by flattening the mutual recursion away with a fueled driver.
